q: Which list names the four primary tissue types?
options: Epithelial, connective, muscle and nervous
Epithelial, glandular, muscle and nervous
Epithelial, connective, skeletal and blood
Squamous, cuboidal, columnar and transitional

q: An epithelial cell's apical surface faces which direction?
options: Toward the basement membrane
Toward the capillaries that supply it
Toward a lumen or the outside of the body
Toward neighboring cells along its sides

q: What does it mean that epithelium is avascular?
options: Its cells have no nuclei
It contains no blood vessels of its own
It cannot divide or renew itself
It is not attached to deeper tissue

q: Under a microscope you see one layer of flat cells lining a small blood vessel. What is this tissue called?
options: Mesothelium
Transitional epithelium
Simple cuboidal epithelium
Endothelium

q: A researcher designs a membrane for an artificial lung. Oxygen must cross it as fast as possible. Which natural epithelium is the best model?
options: Stratified squamous epithelium
Simple columnar epithelium
Simple squamous epithelium
Transitional epithelium

q: In a slide of airway lining, nuclei sit at three different heights, but every cell touches the basement membrane. How should you classify it?
options: Ciliated stratified columnar epithelium
Pseudostratified columnar epithelium
Transitional epithelium
Simple cuboidal epithelium

q: Which features are shared by every epithelium? Select all that apply.
options: Cells joined closely by cell junctions
An apical surface and a basal surface
Blood vessels running between the cells
Attachment to a basement membrane
Several layers of cells

q: Which two layers make up the basement membrane?
options: The apical surface and the basal surface of the cells
The epidermis and the dermis
The basal lamina and the reticular lamina
Endothelium and mesothelium

q: A long-term smoker coughs up mucus every morning. A biopsy shows his tracheal lining has lost its cilia in many places. Which process has failed?
options: Diffusion of oxygen across the tracheal lining
Sweeping of mucus up and out of the airway
Release of mucus by goblet cells
Stretching of the airway lining during breathing

q: The esophagus is lined by nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium. Which description of that lining and its conditions is accurate?
options: Many layers face scraping food, and the moist surface cells stay alive
Its surface cells absorb nutrients from food as it passes
Food passes too quickly to rub the lining
Its surface cells are dead and packed with keratin

q: Put the steps of airway clearing by respiratory epithelium in order.
options: Goblet cells release mucus onto the surface
Inhaled dust and microbes stick to the mucus
Cilia beat in waves toward the throat
The mucus sheet moves up and out of the airway
You swallow the mucus

q: A slide of an empty urinary bladder shows a lining six cells thick with rounded, dome-shaped surface cells. The same tissue from a full bladder looks only two or three cells thick with flat surface cells. What explains the difference?
options: The surface cells flake off as the bladder fills
The full bladder sample came from another region
The cells rearrange and flatten as the wall stretches
Cells in the full bladder lose water to the urine

q: Fill in the missing step. Epithelium has no blood vessels → ______ → the deepest cells of a stratified epithelium, nearest the capillaries, are the best supplied.
options: Diffusion from capillaries below feeds its cells
Its cells make their own glucose from carbon dioxide
Its surface cells absorb what they need from the air or food passing by
Its basement membrane carries blood in channels between the cells

q: This description of how the epidermis renews itself contains one wrong step. Find it.
options: Cells in the deepest layer, nearest the capillaries, divide
Their daughter cells are pushed up toward the surface
The rising cells fill with keratin
The rising cells take in more blood from vessels between them
Surface cells die and flake off, and cells from below replace them

q: Which lining would you expect in a kidney tubule, where cells pull salts and nutrients back out of the fluid passing through by active transport?
options: Keratinized stratified squamous epithelium
Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium
Transitional epithelium
Simple cuboidal epithelium

q: After years of smoking, patches of a man's tracheal lining change from pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium to stratified squamous epithelium. Predict the effect on each variable in those patches.

variables.name: Resistance of the lining to physical irritation
Number of cilia on the surface
Mucus released onto the surface by goblet cells
Clearing of trapped particles from those patches

q: What does a goblet cell release?
options: Keratin
Serous fluid
Mucus
Urine

q: The upper surface of the epiglottis, which food slides across, is covered by which epithelium?
options: Simple squamous epithelium
Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells
Transitional epithelium
Nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium

q: What feature defines connective tissue?
options: Sheets of cells packed edge to edge
Few cells scattered in a large amount of extracellular matrix
Cells that shorten and pull when they are stimulated
A free surface facing a lumen or the outside

q: What are the two parts of the extracellular matrix?
options: Fibroblasts and macrophages
Plasma and platelets
Basal lamina and reticular lamina
Ground substance and fibers

q: Which fiber lets a tissue stretch and then snap back to its resting length?
options: Collagen fiber
Reticular fiber
Elastic fiber
Keratin filament

q: Which cell makes the fibers and ground substance of connective tissue proper?
options: Fibroblast
Macrophage
Adipocyte
Chondrocyte

q: A splinter carries bacteria into the areolar tissue under your skin. Which resident connective tissue cell engulfs the bacteria by phagocytosis?
options: Fibroblast
Adipocyte
Macrophage
Chondrocyte

q: Why does a tendon resist a pull along its length far better than a pull from the side?
options: Its elastic fibers stretch sideways but not lengthwise
Its collagen bundles run parallel to the pull
It has more ground substance than other connective tissues
Its cells contract to resist the force

q: The dermis of your skin is stretched in many directions as you move. Which tissue fits that job?
options: Dense regular connective tissue
Reticular tissue
Hyaline cartilage
Dense irregular tissue

q: Which are forms of loose connective tissue? Select all that apply.
options: Areolar tissue
Adipose tissue
Tendon
Reticular tissue
Fibrocartilage

q: What does a ligament connect?
options: Bone to bone
Muscle to bone
Muscle to muscle
Skin to bone

q: An athlete tears the inner part of a knee meniscus and, in the same month, breaks a bone in her wrist. The bone heals in eight weeks; the meniscus tear does not heal. What best explains the difference?
options: The meniscus is made of elastic cartilage, which tears more easily
Bone has no cells, so it simply sets like cement
The inner meniscus lacks blood vessels; bone has many
Fibrocartilage has a thick perichondrium that blocks healing

q: Which type of cartilage forms the flexible flap of your outer ear?
options: Hyaline cartilage
Fibrocartilage
Articular cartilage
Elastic cartilage

q: An intervertebral disc is squeezed by your body weight and pulled as you bend and twist. Why is it made of fibrocartilage rather than hyaline cartilage?
options: Thick collagen bundles resist pulling too
Fibrocartilage has blood vessels that speed repair
Fibrocartilage is the most flexible type of cartilage
Hyaline cartilage disappears after birth

q: In brown adipose tissue, a mitochondrial protein lets hydrogen ions leak back across the inner membrane without passing through the ATP-making machinery. What is the result?
options: More ATP is made per glucose
The energy is released as heat
The cell stores more triglyceride in one large droplet
Oxygen use stops

q: Put the steps of forming a blood clot (short version) in order.
options: A blood vessel is cut
Platelets stick to the damaged wall and to each other
A protein dissolved in the plasma turns into long, sticky threads
The threads tangle around the platelets and trap red cells
A jelly-like plug seals the leak

q: Blood is classed as a connective tissue. Which part of blood plays the role of the extracellular matrix?
options: Red blood cells
Platelets
Plasma
White blood cells
misconception: blood is not a connective tissue

q: Mesenchyme is best described as what?
options: The layer that wraps most cartilage
Embryonic connective tissue made of stem cells
The protein mat that anchors an epithelium
The heat-making fat found in newborns

q: This description of how cartilage gets its supplies contains one wrong step. Find it.
options: Blood vessels run through the perichondrium around most cartilage
Oxygen and nutrients leave those vessels
Capillaries inside the matrix deliver them to each chondrocyte
Chondrocytes in the center are the farthest from the supply
Repair of damaged cartilage is slow

q: Fill in the missing step. You press on articular cartilage → ______ → the cartilage flattens slightly → when the load lifts, water flows back and it springs back.
options: Water is squeezed out of the ground substance
Elastic fibers in the matrix recoil
Chondrocytes contract
Blood drains out of its capillaries

q: A genetic disorder weakens a person's collagen fibers. Predict the effect on each variable.

variables.name: Strength of tendons and ligaments when pulled
Resistance of the dermis to tearing
Ability of bone to resist bending without breaking

q: Which muscle tissue has long, cylindrical fibers, each with many nuclei pressed against its edge?
options: Smooth muscle tissue
Cardiac muscle tissue
Skeletal muscle tissue
Visceral (smooth) muscle tissue

q: Where are intercalated discs found?
options: Between neighboring cardiac muscle fibers
Between skeletal muscle fibers and their tendon
Inside each smooth muscle fiber
Between the nuclei of a skeletal muscle fiber

q: Which features do skeletal and cardiac muscle tissue share? Select all that apply.
options: Striations
Voluntary control
Actin and myosin filaments
Many nuclei at the edge of each fiber
Intercalated discs

q: A pathologist examines a slide of muscle. The fibers are striated and branched, each has one nucleus in its center, and dark zigzag lines cross the fibers where they meet. Which organ did the sample come from?
options: The biceps in the upper arm
The heart
The wall of the stomach
The wall of the urinary bladder

q: The smooth muscle around a small artery contracts and cuts its radius to half. With the pressure gradient unchanged, what happens to the resistance of that artery?
options: It doubles
It rises to four times its starting value
It rises to 16 times its starting value
It falls to half

q: You step outside without gloves on a freezing day. The smooth muscle in the walls of the small arteries supplying your fingers contracts. Predict the effect on each variable in those arteries and fingers.

variables.name: Resistance to blood flow in those arteries

q: A classmate says, "If a muscle is striated, it must be under voluntary control." Which tissue shows the claim is wrong?
options: Skeletal muscle of the thigh
Smooth muscle of the intestine
Smooth muscle of a blood vessel
Cardiac muscle of the heart

q: This description of how a region of the heart wall contracts together contains one wrong step. Find it.
options: One cardiac fiber produces an electrical change across its membrane
Ions carrying the change pass through desmosomes into the next fiber
The next fiber undergoes the same electrical change and contracts
The change spreads fiber by fiber across the region
Desmosomes hold the fibers together as they pull on each other

q: Put the steps of vasoconstriction in a small artery in order.
options: Smooth muscle fibers in the vessel wall contract
The ring of muscle around the vessel tightens
The vessel's radius shrinks
Resistance to blood flow rises
Blood flow through that vessel falls

q: Fill in the missing step. A cardiac fiber undergoes an electrical change → ______ → the neighboring fiber undergoes the same change → the neighbor contracts.
options: Ions flow into the neighbor through gap junctions
Desmosomes pull the neighbor's membrane toward the first fiber
The neighbor fuses with the first fiber
A tendon passes the pull on to the neighbor

q: Your stomach wall stretches well beyond its resting size after a large meal without being damaged. Which property of muscle tissue does this show?
options: Elasticity
Extensibility
Responsiveness
Ability to contract

q: A strip of smooth muscle from a bladder wall is stretched in a lab dish and then released, with no stimulus. It returns to its resting length. Which property of muscle tissue is at work?
options: Extensibility
Responsiveness
Elasticity
Voluntary control

q: Months after part of Ray's heart wall died from lack of blood, the patch is still thin, stiff and does not contract. A thigh muscle torn in a fall, by contrast, regains most of its function. What best explains the difference?
options: Cardiac muscle has no blood supply to reach the damage
Adult cardiac fibers almost never divide, so collagen fills the gap
Cardiac fibers are nonstriated and cannot rebuild their filaments
Skeletal muscle is voluntary, and practice regrows its fibers

q: Which of these is lined with smooth muscle tissue?
options: The wall of the intestines
The muscle that bends your elbow
The wall of the heart
The muscles that move your eyes

q: Smooth muscle contains actin and myosin, just as skeletal muscle does. Why does it show no striations?
options: Its many nuclei hide the bands
Involuntary muscle does not form stripes
Its filaments crisscross instead of lining up
It contains no myosin, only actin

q: Which muscle tissues are involuntary? Select all that apply.
options: Skeletal muscle tissue
Cardiac muscle tissue
Smooth muscle tissue

q: When you straighten your bent elbow, the muscle on the front of your arm does not push the forearm straight. Why not?
options: It is too weak to push against gravity
Pushing needs more ATP than it has
It relaxes whenever the arm is bent
A shortening fiber can pull but not push

q: A newborn's thigh muscle fibers each contain hundreds of nuclei. How did one fiber come to have so many?
options: Many embryonic cells fused together into one fiber
Its nucleus divided many times without the cell dividing
Stem cells beside it pushed their nuclei into it after birth
Nuclei from the blood entered the fiber

q: A drug blocks the gap junctions in the intercalated discs of the heart but leaves the desmosomes intact. What would you expect?
options: The fibers would pull apart as they contract
The fibers would contract out of step
The fibers would lose their striations
The heart would contract more strongly than normal

q: Which two kinds of cells make up nervous tissue?
options: Neurons and fibroblasts
Neurons and glial cells
Glial cells and muscle fibers
Nerves and axons

q: Which part of a neuron is specialized to receive signals from other cells?
options: The axon
The axon terminals
The dendrites
The nucleus

q: Which way does an axon carry a neuron's signal?
options: From the dendrites into the cell body
Away from the cell body toward the axon terminals
From the axon terminals back to the cell body
In either direction, depending on where the signal starts

q: Put the path of a signal through one neuron in order.
options: Dendrites receive signals from other cells
The cell body combines the incoming signals
The axon carries a signal away from the cell body
Axon terminals release chemicals onto the next cell

q: Which part of a neuron holds its nucleus and makes nearly all of its proteins?
options: The axon
The dendrites
The axon terminals
The cell body

q: After a deep cut at his wrist, Jamal's thumb and first two fingers are numb, and he also cannot move his thumb across his palm. Why did one cut cause both problems?
options: The cut nerve held axons carrying signals in both directions
The cut destroyed the neurons' cell bodies in his wrist
Only the muscles were cut, and numbness follows muscle injury
Glial cells in the wrist stopped making the signals

q: Which description fits a nerve?
options: A single, very long neuron
The cell body and dendrites of one neuron
A bundle of many axons wrapped in connective tissue
A cluster of glial cells inside the brain
misconception: a nerve is a single neuron

q: Which of these are jobs of glial cells? Select all that apply.
options: Wrapping axons in layers of membrane that insulate them
Carrying long-distance signals from the spinal cord to the toes
Controlling the makeup of the fluid around neurons
Engulfing dead cells and microbes
Holding neurons in place

q: A 45-year-old woman has a cancerous tumor that began in her brain tissue. From which cells did it most likely grow?
options: Neurons
Fibroblasts
Nerves
Glial cells

q: This description of how a signal passes through a neuron contains one wrong step. Find it.
options: Dendrites receive signals from other neurons
The cell body combines the incoming signals
The axon carries the signal toward the cell body
Axon terminals release chemicals by exocytosis
The next cell responds to the chemicals

q: Fill in the missing step. An axon is cut in the forearm → ______ → the part of the axon beyond the cut breaks down within days.
options: That part loses its supply of proteins from the cell body
That part takes in a new nucleus from the glial cells nearby
Blood floods into the axon and dissolves it
The cell body releases chemicals that dissolve it

q: A man's heart stops for six minutes before it is restarted. His heart muscle and skin recover, but he has lasting brain damage. Which features of neurons best explain why they were hurt most?
options: They are wrapped by glial cells that block oxygen
They have many nuclei that need extra glucose
They are avascular and depend on diffusion
They store little fuel, use a lot of oxygen and do not divide

q: One kind of neuron in the brain has an enormous tree of dendrite branches. What does that structure allow it to do?
options: Carry its signal farther
Divide more often
Release chemicals from the tips of its dendrites
Receive signals from many other neurons

q: What happens at an axon terminal (synaptic end bulb) when a signal arrives?
options: It releases chemicals by exocytosis onto the next cell
It sends the signal back toward the cell body
It divides to form a new neuron
It holds on to the signal until the neuron is at rest again

q: A disease destroys the glial wrapping around the axons in one region, but leaves the axons themselves intact at first. Predict the effect on each variable for those axons.

variables.name: Speed of signals along the axons
Number of axons in the region (at first)
Time for a signal to reach the axon terminals

q: The name dendrite comes from a root that describes its shape. What does dendr- mean?
options: Tree
Axis
Glue
Nerve

q: What do direct counts of whole human brains show about the numbers of glial cells and neurons?
options: Glial cells outnumber neurons about ten to one
Neurons outnumber glial cells about ten to one
The brain has roughly equal numbers of each
The adult brain has no glial cells left
misconception: glia outnumber neurons ten to one

q: A small sample of a nerve from the leg is examined under a microscope. What will it contain?
options: The cell bodies of the neurons whose axons it carries
One very large neuron running the length of the leg
Axons, glial cells, connective tissue and small blood vessels
Cardiac muscle fibers that move signals along
misconception: a nerve is a single neuron
